Patient Vignette: "Kwame"

Kwame is a 23-year-old urban planner who presents as a tall, thoughtful young man, his posture rigid and his eyes scanning the room as he settles into the chair. He speaks in measured, deliberate sentences, often pausing to check the corners of the office before continuing. He has been referred by his primary care physician after reporting persistent insomnia and an inability to concentrate at work.

The story begins eleven months ago, on a Tuesday evening in late October. Kwame had stayed late at the city planning office, finalizing a transit-oriented development proposal for a neighborhood he had grown up visiting. He remembers feeling proud—this was the kind of project that made him feel his work mattered. He left the office around 9:30 PM, walking the six blocks to the metro station, a route he had taken hundreds of times. The streets were quiet, the air cool and damp. As he passed an alley between a shuttered laundromat and a bodega, two men stepped out. One grabbed his arm; the other pressed something hard against his ribs. He remembers the smell of cigarette smoke and cheap cologne, the sound of his own breathing, the feeling of his wallet being pulled from his back pocket. They demanded his phone. He gave it. Then one of them hit him—a single, brutal punch to the side of his head. He fell. They kicked him twice, once in the ribs, once in the back. Then they were gone. He lay on the wet pavement for what felt like a long time, staring at a crushed soda can, listening to his own ragged breath.

Kwame called his older sister from a payphone. She drove him to the emergency room, where X-rays showed no fractures, only deep bruises and a mild concussion. The police took a report. They never found the men. For the first few weeks, Kwame told himself he was fine. He went back to work after three days, determined not to let "some random act" define him. But he noticed changes. He stopped taking the metro. He started driving to work, even though it added forty minutes to his commute. He began mapping his routes—literally, in his head, like a planner—identifying every alley, every dark corner, every place someone could hide. He started avoiding the neighborhood where the project was located, delegating site visits to a junior colleague.

Now, eleven months later, the world has shrunk. Kwame lives in a small studio apartment on the third floor of a building with a secure entry. He has not walked anywhere after dark in over nine months. At work, his colleagues have noticed his distraction. He struggles to focus during meetings, his eyes darting to the windows. He has missed three deadlines. His supervisor, a patient woman who once mentored him, has placed him on a performance improvement plan. Kwame feels a deep, corrosive shame about this. He was the rising star, the young planner with the big ideas. Now he sits at his desk, unable to read a zoning map without his heart racing.

He sleeps poorly. When he does sleep, he dreams of the alley, but in the dreams, the men are always his colleagues, or his father, or strangers with familiar faces. He wakes gasping, his hands clenched. He has started drinking—two or three beers most nights, sometimes more on weekends—to quiet the hypervigilance. He has not dated anyone since the assault. He canceled on a woman he met at a conference, making an excuse about a work emergency. The truth was, he couldn't bear the thought of being outside after dark with someone else, of her seeing him flinch at a car backfiring.

Kwame tells me he feels like he is "planning around a hole in the ground." He says his life used to feel like a map with clear destinations—a career, a family, a future. Now, he says, the map has a black spot where the alley used to be, and everything else has to be routed around it. He cannot see beyond it. He is tired. He is ashamed. And he is here, he says, because he is afraid he is losing the person he was supposed to become.
